title: Prior Restraint
short: Orders that stop speech before it happens bear a heavy presumption against validity: Near v. Minnesota (1931) struck down a law allowing newspapers to be shut down; New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), the Pentagon Papers case, refused to block publication.
trouble: Students think the Pentagon Papers decision was one opinion of the Court. It was a short per curiam with nine separate opinions; it says the government did not meet its heavy burden.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

A prior restraint stops speech before it happens: a court order not to publish, or a license required before speaking. English writers such as Blackstone saw freedom of the press as, at its core, freedom from prior restraints. The Court has made such restraints the most suspect form of control over speech, more so than punishment after the fact for defamation or other harms.

opts.facts: Minnesota's "public nuisance" law let a judge shut down a "malicious, scandalous and defamatory" newspaper. Jay Near's Saturday Press, which accused Minneapolis officials of ties to gangsters and was filled with bigoted attacks, was ordered closed.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Hughes wrote that the law was "the essence of censorship." Officials could sue for libel afterward, but not stop the paper in advance. He named narrow exceptions, such as publishing the sailing dates of transports or the number and location of troops in wartime.

opts.facts: In 1971 the New York Times and the Washington Post began publishing a classified study of U.S. decision-making in Vietnam, leaked by Daniel Ellsberg. The government sought orders to stop publication, citing national security.
opts.reasoning: In a short per curiam opinion, the Court said that "any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity," and that the government had not met its heavy burden. Each of the nine justices wrote separately, with different views of when, if ever, a restraint could issue.

blocks.html: Why single out prior restraints? A punishment after publication comes after a trial, with the speech already in the open where people can judge it. A restraint stops ideas before anyone hears them, often on a quick hearing and a judge's prediction of harm. Courts treat gag orders on the press about pending trials the same way: they are presumed invalid when other measures could protect a fair trial. Prior restraint doctrine does not mean the press can never be punished: the Pentagon Papers ruling left open whether criminal laws could apply after publication.

events.label: New York Times Co. v. United States

blocks.html: Prior restraints carry a heavy presumption against validity: Near v. Minnesota (1931) struck down a law allowing newspapers to be shut down; in New York Times Co. v. United States (1971) (the Pentagon Papers) the government did not meet its heavy burden. Narrow exceptions (such as troop movements in wartime) were named in Near.

blocks.title: A court order
blocks.q: A judge orders a TV station not to air an interview about a city contract until after the next election, saying it might mislead voters. Valid?
steps: This is a prior restraint: it stops speech in advance.
The reason (it might mislead) is far from the narrow exceptions like wartime troop movements.
The heavy presumption against validity is not overcome.

blocks.title: How many opinions?
blocks.q: How was the Pentagon Papers case decided, in form?
steps: A short per curiam opinion for the Court, 6 to 3.
Every justice wrote separately: six concurrences and three dissents.
blocks.a: A short per curiam plus nine separate opinions.

blocks.html: Thinking the Pentagon Papers decision was one opinion of the Court. It was a short per curiam with nine separate opinions; what it holds is that the government did not meet its heavy burden. It did not decide whether publishers could be punished afterward.
